His opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, trained as a doctor and a former public- health director, won his party's primary by about one point. The Cook Political Report calls the race a toss-up; two other forecasters give Democrats a slight edge. Spending on the race has already set a state record. How did Michigan get here? How did Michigan become a swing state? Its politics have long been shaped by the car and the union. Michigan claims the birthplace of the Republican Party, at a meeting under the oaks in Jackson in 1854. A century later, Macomb County, north of Detroit, gave John F. Kennedy sixty-three percent; in 1984 it gave Ronald Reagan sixty-six. The pollster Stan Greenberg was sent to find out why, and made Macomb's Reagan Democrats famous. From 1992 to 2012, Michigan voted Democratic for president six times in a row. Then, in 2016, Donald Trump carried it by ten thousand seven hundred and four votes, the closest result in the country. Joe Biden won it back in 2020 by a hundred and fifty-four thousand; Trump took it again in 2024 by eighty thousand. What divides Michigan's voters? Geography, first. Wayne County, home to Detroit, gave Kamala Harris a margin of twenty-nine points in 2024. Washtenaw and Ingham, home to the University of Michigan and Michigan State, voted Democratic by even more. Oakland, the affluent suburbs north of Detroit, voted Democratic by eleven points; its neighbour Macomb, Republican by fourteen. West Michigan, where Dutch Reformed immigrants settled in the eighteen hundreds, has long been Republican: Ottawa County by twenty points. But Kent, around Grand Rapids, has voted Democratic for president since 2020. Across the Upper Peninsula and the rural north, most counties vote Republican by wide margins. And labour still counts here: thirteen percent of Michigan workers belong to a union, against ten percent nationally. Where have the votes been moving? In both directions at once. Between 2016 and 2024, Kent and Oakland moved toward Democrats, while Macomb and Genesee, around Flint, moved toward Republicans. Returning to Macomb in 2018, Greenberg said its voters 'gave Donald Trump his margin in Michigan.' In 2024, the war in Gaza moved votes too. In Dearborn, where most residents report Middle Eastern or North African ancestry, unofficial results gave Trump forty-two percent, Kamala Harris thirty-six, and the Green candidate, Jill Stein, eighteen. And many Michiganders split their tickets. Rogers ran a hundred and twenty-three thousand votes behind Trump, and lost to Slotkin by nineteen thousand. As the political scientist Matt Grossmann put it, very few voters chose both Slotkin and Trump, 'but it was more than the voters selecting Kamala Harris and Mike Rogers.' What issues move Michigan voters? First, the cost of living, and the car. In 2025 a twenty-five percent federal tariff on imported cars and light trucks was imposed. El-Sayed backs 'targeted, smart tariffs'; Rogers now says, 'We need to end this tariff war now.' Second, health care. El-Sayed campaigns for Medicare for All; Rogers says, 'You deserve to know the price before you get the bill.' Third, abortion: in 2022, almost fifty-seven percent of voters wrote abortion rights into the state constitution. Fourth, war abroad. El-Sayed does not want tax dollars 'used to subsidize war abroad'; on the conflict with Iran, Rogers says, 'We need it to come to an end.' And faith: in a Pew survey, thirty-one percent of Michigan adults had no religious affiliation, and fifty-nine percent were Christian. How did they win their nominations? Peters announced his retirement in January 2025. Rogers entered the race that April; in July, President Trump endorsed him, and no other Republican qualified for the primary ballot. The Democratic contest was one of the most expensive Senate primaries in American history: Bridge Michigan counted ninety- eight million dollars in advertising, most of it paid for by outside groups. Congresswoman Haley Stevens was backed by Governor Whitmer and Senator Peters; El-Sayed by Senator Bernie Sanders and the United Auto Workers. State Senator Mallory McMorrow withdrew in July. On the fourth of August, El-Sayed won by about one point. Stevens conceded: 'I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election.' The four smaller parties chose their nominees at conventions. Who is Abdul El-Sayed? He was born in Michigan in 1984, the son of an Egyptian immigrant father. He studied at the University of Michigan, was a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford, where he earned a doctorate, and took a medical degree at Columbia; he did not complete a residency, and is not licensed to practise. At thirty, he became Detroit's health director. In 2018 he ran for governor and finished second to Whitmer. Later he led Wayne County's health department. In his own words: 'It's way too hard to survive here in the richest, most powerful country in the world and it should not be this hard to get by.' His slogan: 'Money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for All.' On abortion, he says decisions about your body and your health 'belong to you, not politicians.' What do his critics say, and how does he answer? El-Sayed's critics focus on his health plan and on remarks after an attack. In the primary, McMorrow said the Medicare for All bill he champions 'completely eliminates private health insurance as it exists today.' At the debate, Rogers said he was selling 'the best con I think I've ever seen.' His campaign answers that he wants 'guaranteed public health insurance for every American. Cradle to grave.' In March, a man drove a car into Temple Israel, a synagogue in West Bloomfield, and fired at a guard. El-Sayed condemned the attack, but also said 'hurt people hurt people'. Rogers said he 'has had six months to apologize for his incredibly horrific remarks.' In August, El-Sayed said: 'I made a mistake.' Who is Mike Rogers? He was born in Livonia in 1963 and grew up in Livingston County. He served as an Army officer and then as an FBI special agent in Chicago, working on public-corruption and organised-crime cases. He was elected to the Michigan Senate in 1994, and in 2000 won a seat in Congress by one hundred and eleven votes. He served fourteen years in the House, chairing the Intelligence Committee from 2011. After Congress he worked as a television commentator and in cyber-security. In 2024 he lost the Senate race to Slotkin by nineteen thousand votes. In his own words: 'As Michigan's senator, I'll bring both parties together to lower your prices. That's job No. 1.' On drug prices, he says Michigan should not pay more than Canada; on abortion he said in 2024: 'Michigan voters have already decided the issue, and I respect that decision.' What do his critics say, and how does he answer? Rogers's critics focus on where he has lived, and on tariffs. After leaving Congress, he and his wife bought a home in Florida and claimed it as their primary residence in 2023. El-Sayed says: 'If you want to be a Florida man, go be a Florida man.' The state Democratic chair, Curtis Hertel, said: 'He left us, and he left the people that he served.' Rogers's campaign answers: 'Mike Rogers will be a senator for Michigan.' Bridge Michigan found that he now lives and votes in Michigan. On tariffs, in August Rogers called them 'necessary when countries cheat American workers'; in October, an advertisement said, 'We need to end this tariff war now.' El- Sayed calls it flip-flopping. Rogers answers: 'There are tariffs that I think are too high and not helpful for us.' Who else is on the ballot? Six names. Lydia Christensen, a technology founder from Ironwood, in the Upper Peninsula, is the Libertarian nominee. Walter P. Kristy, vice chair of the Natural Law Party of Michigan, is that party's nominee. Tim Long, of Taylor, in Wayne County, represents the U.S. Taxpayers Party. Douglas P. Marsh is the Green nominee again; in 2024 he won almost fifty-four thousand votes, about one percent. Two years ago, the candidates of the smaller parties together won about a hundred and seventy thousand votes, nine times Slotkin's margin over Rogers. Michigan voters can still register in person, with proof of residency, up to and on Election Day. What happened in the first debate? On the eighth of October in Grand Rapids, the candidates argued so hard they kept going through a commercial break. The moderator, Rick Albin, said he had never seen that in thirty years. El-Sayed said the race is 'about whether you can afford your gas, your groceries, and can see a doctor.' Rogers answered: 'We cannot afford Abdul.' Fact-checkers have found false claims on both sides. PolitiFact rated El-Sayed's claim that Rogers took a fourteen-million-dollar payout as a pharmaceutical lobbyist 'Pants on Fire', and Rogers's claim that El-Sayed 'can't condemn' the synagogue attack 'Mostly False'. Behind the debate is money: by the end of September, El-Sayed had raised twice as much, but Rogers had more cash in hand. A second and final debate, on Detroit's WXYZ, was held on the twenty-first of October. What do the polls say? In July, a Glengariff poll had Rogers ahead by about ten points, and in August a Fox News poll had him ahead by four. Since the primary, most polls show a close race with a narrow El-Sayed lead. The New York Times and Siena, interviewing six hundred and five likely voters from the fifteenth to the twenty- second of September, found El-Sayed ahead forty-nine to forty-four, with a margin of error of four point nine. Fox News found fifty to forty-nine. Glengariff, for The Detroit News and WDIV, had Rogers ahead by one point four. InsiderAdvantage, on the ninth and tenth of October, found forty-eight to forty-six, and Rasmussen Reports forty-six to forty-four. The newest, Marist, from the fifteenth to the eighteenth, found fifty to forty-eight among likely voters. The FiftyPlusOne average gives El-Sayed about three points. Many of these leads are within the margin of error. A poll is a snapshot, not a forecast. What should you watch on election night? Early in-person voting runs from the twenty-fourth of October to the first of November. Then, first, Macomb County: in 2024 it voted for Trump by almost fourteen points, but for Rogers by under ten. Second, Kent and Oakland, suburban counties that have moved toward Democrats. Third, turnout in Wayne County, home to Detroit and Dearborn. Fourth, the Upper Peninsula and the rural north, where Republicans win most counties by wide margins. The polls close at eight in the evening, local time; the western Upper Peninsula, on Central time, closes an hour after the rest of the state. Two nominees offer Michigan very different answers on health care, trade and war abroad, in a state whose last two statewide federal races were decided by less than two points. Whoever wins will take the seat Gary Peters has held since 2015, and may help decide who controls the Senate. On the third of November, Michigan votes. title: California Governor Race 2026: Becerra vs Hilton Explained
description_snippet: The 2026 California governor's race explained (elección para gobernador de California 2026): Xavier Becerra (D) vs Steve Hilton ...

transcript: On the third of November, 2026, California chooses a governor. It is the most populous state in the country, and for the first time since 2018 the office is open: Gavin Newsom has served the two terms the law allows. No Republican has won a statewide race in California since 2006, and the forecasters rate this one solidly Democratic. Yet the ballot holds just two names, one from each party. Xavier Becerra, sixty-eight, the Democrat: born in Sacramento, a congressman for twenty-four years, then attorney general and Secretary of Health and Human Services, endorsed by Governor Newsom. Steve Hilton, fifty-seven, the Republican: born in London, once a strategist for a British prime minister, later a Fox News host, endorsed by President Trump. In June, sixty-one candidates ran in a single primary. How did these two reach the final? How did California become a Democratic state? It was not always one. Ronald Reagan governed it from 1967 to 1975, and California voted Republican for president in six straight elections, from 1968 to 1988. In 1978, almost sixty-five percent of voters approved Proposition 13, which capped property taxes. In 1994, fifty-nine percent approved Proposition 187, to deny many public services to undocumented immigrants; the courts blocked most of it. Gary Segura, then a Stanford political scientist, counted about a million new Latino voters by 2000; how much that changed the state's politics is still debated. Since 1992, California has voted Democratic for president every time. Arnold Schwarzenegger, elected in the 2003 recall and re-elected in 2006, was the last Republican elected governor. How does California's primary work? In 2010, voters approved Proposition 14 with fifty-four percent. Since then, every candidate for governor appears on one primary ballot, and every voter may choose any of them. The top two advance to November, whatever their party, and write-in candidates are not allowed in the final round. In theory, two Democrats, or two Republicans, could face each other. In every race for governor so far, it has been one of each. This year, with so many Democrats running, some Democrats feared that two Republicans might finish first and second. In April the Republican strategist Rob Stutzman said of Hilton and Sheriff Chad Bianco that 'they need to beat each other but they both need to succeed at the same time.' That month President Trump endorsed Hilton, but at the state party's convention neither man won the sixty percent needed for its endorsement. How did a Republican reach the final two? On the second of June, sixty-one candidates were on the ballot: twenty-four Democrats, twelve Republicans and twenty-five others. Becerra finished first with twenty-eight percent, and Hilton second with almost twenty-five. Tom Steyer, a Democrat whose campaign spent about two hundred and fifteen million dollars, came third with twenty-three. Democratic candidates won sixty-two percent of the vote between them, but split it many ways; Republican candidates won thirty-six percent, almost all of it shared by two men. Hilton led in thirty-four of the fifty- eight counties, and on election night he briefly led statewide, until more mail ballots were counted. A week later Steyer conceded: 'It would be a travesty for Steve Hilton to win the governorship.' Governor Newsom, neutral during the primary, then endorsed Becerra. Where are California's votes? About a quarter of them are cast in Los Angeles County alone, and the coast, from San Diego to the Bay Area, votes heavily Democratic. Inland, the picture changes. In 2024, Kamala Harris won her home state by twenty points, down from Joe Biden's twenty-nine. Donald Trump carried ten counties that had voted for Biden, among them Fresno, Riverside, San Bernardino and Imperial, on the Mexican border; as CalMatters noted, mostly because fewer people voted for Harris. Yet in the 2021 recall, sixty-two percent had voted to keep Governor Newsom. In September, the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies found Becerra ahead in Orange County and the Inland Empire, and Hilton ahead in the San Joaquin Valley. What do California's voters want? A record twenty-three point two million are registered: forty-five percent Democrats, twenty-five percent Republicans, and twenty-three percent with no party preference. In the Public Policy Institute of California's survey in May, forty-four percent named the cost of living as the state's most important issue, and fourteen percent housing. On housing, Becerra promises to declare the shortage 'a state of emergency' on his first day; Hilton promises to 'clear out the red tape, fees and bad rules'. On gasoline, Hilton promises three-dollar gas, though he says the Middle East makes it 'hard to get exactly to that'; Becerra wants to work with the refineries 'so they can continue to provide the gasoline'. On high-speed rail, Hilton would cancel it; Becerra would 'scrap the current configuration' and finish it. Who is Xavier Becerra? He was born in Sacramento in 1958; his father was a construction worker, and his mother had immigrated from Jalisco, in Mexico. He was the first in his family to earn a university degree, at Stanford, where he also studied law. From 1993 he represented Los Angeles in Congress for twelve terms. In 2017 he became California's attorney general, and, his office said, took the first Trump administration to court a hundred and twenty-two times. In 2021 the Senate confirmed him as Secretary of Health and Human Services, fifty votes to forty-nine. In his own words, 'The California Dream is slipping away.' He promises a housing emergency, to tie 'every dollar' of homelessness spending 'to results', and to 'protect and lead our state against Trump and his attacks.' What do his critics say, and how does he answer? Two issues stand out. The first is his department's care of migrant children who crossed the border alone. In 2023 a New York Times investigation, later awarded a Pulitzer Prize, reported such children working in dangerous jobs, and a federal audit found gaps in background checks. In the debate, Hilton said Becerra had 'dismantled the vetting'. Becerra answers that what happened after children left federal care 'was not on my watch.' The second: about two hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars was taken from his dormant campaign account. Governor Newsom's former chief of staff, Becerra's own former chief of staff and a lobbyist have admitted their roles; Becerra was not charged. His primary rival Antonio Villaraigosa said it 'doesn't pass the smell test.' Becerra says: 'I was not involved.' Who is Steve Hilton? He was born in London in 1969 to Hungarian parents who had fled communism. He won a scholarship to a boarding school, then studied at Oxford. From 2010 to 2012 he was director of strategy to Prime Minister David Cameron. In 2012 he moved to California, as a visiting scholar at Stanford, and co-founded a political crowdfunding start-up. From 2017 to 2023 he hosted a weekly Fox News programme. He became a United States citizen in 2021, and lives in Atherton, in Silicon Valley. In his own words, 'My mission is clear: to go to Sacramento, clean up the corruption, cut your costs, help your business, and fix our schools.' He promises no state income tax on the first hundred and fifty thousand dollars, three-dollar gas, and a Highway Patrol growing toward ten thousand officers. What do his critics say, and how does he answer? They focus on his ties to President Trump. Hilton endorsed Mr. Trump in 2016, while still a British citizen, and on Fox News, CalMatters reports, he called for an audit of the 2020 election. In 2025 he sued to block Proposition 50, the new congressional map; a federal judge found he lacked standing, and he dropped the case. In April, President Trump gave him his 'complete and total endorsement'. Becerra's spokesman calls Mr. Trump 'the albatross around his neck'. Hilton's advertisements answer: 'this election is not about who you hate in Washington. It's about what you love here.' In the debate Becerra said: 'You seem to welcome immigrants who look like you, but deport immigrants who look like me.' Hilton replied: 'What a disgraceful remark that was.' What happened when they met? On the thirtieth of September, in a CNN studio in Burbank, they held what is likely to be their only debate, moderated by Jake Tapper and Dana Bash. Hilton set out his tax plan: no state income tax on the first hundred and fifty thousand dollars, and a flat eight percent above it. Becerra answered: 'You're going to end up with Trump results if you follow Steve Hilton's plan.' Hilton replied: 'All you ever say is Trump, Trump, Trump,' and said Becerra was offering 'more of the same, backed by the same corrupt machine in Sacramento.' Becerra pointed to experience: 'you can't do it with someone who's never served.' Fact-checkers at CapRadio and KPBS rated Hilton's claim about migrant children partly accurate but overstated, and Becerra's claim that Hilton wanted every farm worker deported inaccurate. What do the polls and the money say? Every published poll since the primary shows Becerra ahead. The Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies, with the Los Angeles Times, interviewed four thousand five hundred and twelve likely voters from the fifteenth to the twentieth of September, and found Becerra ahead, fifty-eight to thirty-three. The Public Policy Institute of California found sixty to thirty-eight. Two polls finished in early October: one for the Manhattan Institute found fifty-five to thirty-eight, one for the Independent Voter Project forty-eight to thirty-eight. Two polls for Hilton's campaign found a closer race, with gaps of six and eight points. By mid-October, Becerra had raised forty point five million dollars in all and Hilton twenty- nine million, and outside groups have spent far more for Becerra. A poll is a snapshot, not a forecast. What should you watch on election night? Ballots were mailed to every active registered voter from the fifth of October. The registration deadline was the nineteenth, but Californians can still register and vote conditionally up to Election Day. Ballots postmarked by the third of November count if they arrive within seven days, so counting takes weeks, and leads can move: in the primary, Hilton briefly led on election night. The Berkeley poll found in-person voters favouring Hilton, sixty-two to thirty-one, and mail voters favouring Becerra, sixty- three to twenty-seven. Watch the Central Valley, where Hilton led the primary; Orange County, which he also led; and the Inland Empire, which voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 but for Becerra in the primary. The result is certified by the eleventh of December. Two candidates, one born in Sacramento to a mother from Mexico, the other born in London to Hungarian refugees, offer Californians different answers on taxes, housing, energy and the state's dealings with Washington. Whoever wins will govern the most populous state from January 2027. On the third of November, California decides. transcript: So I've been an AI researcher for over a decade. And a couple of months ago, I got the weirdest email of my career. A random stranger wrote to me saying that my work in AI is going to end humanity. Now I get it, AI, it's so hot right now. (Laughter) It's in the headlines pretty much every day, sometimes because of really cool things like discovering new molecules for medicine or that dope Pope in the white puffer coat. But other times the headlines have been really dark, like that chatbot telling that guy that he should divorce his wife or that AI meal planner app proposing a crowd pleasing recipe featuring chlorine gas. And in the background, we've heard a lot of talk about doomsday scenarios, existential risk and the singularity, with letters being written and events being organized to make sure that doesn't happen. Now I'm a researcher who studies AI's impacts on society, and I don't know what's going to happen in 10 or 20 years, and nobody really does. But what I do know is that there's some pretty nasty things going on right now, because AI doesn't exist in a vacuum. It is part of society, and it has impacts on people and the planet. AI models can contribute to climate change. Their training data uses art and books created by artists and authors without their consent. And its deployment can discriminate against entire communities. But we need to start tracking its impacts. We need to start being transparent and disclosing them and creating tools so that people understand AI better, so that hopefully future generations of AI models are going to be more trustworthy, sustainable, maybe less likely to kill us, if that's what you're into. But let's start with sustainability, because that cloud that AI models live on is actually made out of metal, plastic, and powered by vast amounts of energy. And each time you query an AI model, it comes with a cost to the planet. Last year, I was part of the BigScience initiative, which brought together a thousand researchers from all over the world to create Bloom, the first open large language model, like ChatGPT, but with an emphasis on ethics, transparency and consent. And the study I led that looked at Bloom's environmental impacts found that just training it used as much energy as 30 homes in a whole year and emitted 25 tons of carbon dioxide, which is like driving your car five times around the planet just so somebody can use this model to tell a knock-knock joke. And this might not seem like a lot, but other similar large language models, like GPT-3, emit 20 times more carbon. But the thing is, tech companies aren't measuring this stuff. They're not disclosing it. And so this is probably only the tip of the iceberg, even if it is a melting one. And in recent years we've seen AI models balloon in size because the current trend in AI is "bigger is better." But please don't get me started on why that's the case. In any case, we've seen large language models in particular grow 2,000 times in size over the last five years. And of course, their environmental costs are rising as well. The most recent work I led, found that switching out a smaller, more efficient model for a larger language model emits 14 times more carbon for the same task. Like telling that knock-knock joke. And as we're putting in these models into cell phones and search engines and smart fridges and speakers, the environmental costs are really piling up quickly. So instead of focusing on some future existential risks, let's talk about current tangible impacts and tools we can create to measure and mitigate these impacts. I helped create CodeCarbon, a tool that runs in parallel to AI training code that estimates the amount of energy it consumes and the amount of carbon it emits. And using a tool like this can help us make informed choices, like choosing one model over the other because it's more sustainable, or deploying AI models on renewable energy, which can drastically reduce their emissions. But let's talk about other things because there's other impacts of AI apart from sustainability. For example, it's been really hard for artists and authors to prove that their life's work has been used for training AI models without their consent. And if you want to sue someone, you tend to need proof, right? So Spawning.ai, an organization that was founded by artists, created this really cool tool called “Have I Been Trained?” And it lets you search these massive data sets to see what they have on you. Now, I admit it, I was curious. I searched LAION-5B, which is this huge data set of images and text, to see if any images of me were in there. Now those two first images, that's me from events I've spoken at. But the rest of the images, none of those are me. They're probably of other women named Sasha who put photographs of themselves up on the internet. And this can probably explain why, when I query an image generation model to generate a photograph of a woman named Sasha, more often than not I get images of bikini models. Sometimes they have two arms, sometimes they have three arms, but they rarely have any clothes on. And while it can be interesting for people like you and me to search these data sets, for artists like Karla Ortiz, this provides crucial evidence that her life's work, her artwork, was used for training AI models without her consent, and she and two artists used this as evidence to file a class action lawsuit against AI companies for copyright infringement. And most recently -- (Applause) And most recently Spawning.ai partnered up with Hugging Face, the company where I work at, to create opt-in and opt-out mechanisms for creating these data sets. Because artwork created by humans shouldn’t be an all-you-can-eat buffet for training AI language models. (Applause) The very last thing I want to talk about is bias. You probably hear about this a lot. Formally speaking, it's when AI models encode patterns and beliefs that can represent stereotypes or racism and sexism. One of my heroes, Dr. Joy Buolamwini, experienced this firsthand when she realized that AI systems wouldn't even detect her face unless she was wearing a white-colored mask. Digging deeper, she found that common facial recognition systems were vastly worse for women of color compared to white men. And when biased models like this are deployed in law enforcement settings, this can result in false accusations, even wrongful imprisonment, which we've seen happen to multiple people in recent months. For example, Porcha Woodruff was wrongfully accused of carjacking at eight months pregnant because an AI system wrongfully identified her. But sadly, these systems are black boxes, and even their creators can't say exactly why they work the way they do. And for example, for image generation systems, if they're used in contexts like generating a forensic sketch based on a description of a perpetrator, they take all those biases and they spit them back out for terms like dangerous criminal, terrorists or gang member, which of course is super dangerous when these tools are deployed in society. And so in order to understand these tools better, I created this tool called the Stable Bias Explorer, which lets you explore the bias of image generation models through the lens of professions. So try to picture a scientist in your mind. Don't look at me. What do you see? A lot of the same thing, right? Men in glasses and lab coats. And none of them look like me. And the thing is, is that we looked at all these different image generation models and found a lot of the same thing: significant representation of whiteness and masculinity across all 150 professions that we looked at, even if compared to the real world, the US Labor Bureau of Statistics. These models show lawyers as men, and CEOs as men, almost 100 percent of the time, even though we all know not all of them are white and male. And sadly, my tool hasn't been used to write legislation yet. But I recently presented it at a UN event about gender bias as an example of how we can make tools for people from all walks of life, even those who don't know how to code, to engage with and better understand AI because we use professions, but you can use any terms that are of interest to you. And as these models are being deployed, are being woven into the very fabric of our societies, our cell phones, our social media feeds, even our justice systems and our economies have AI in them. And it's really important that AI stays accessible so that we know both how it works and when it doesn't work. And there's no single solution for really complex things like bias or copyright or climate change. But by creating tools to measure AI's impact, we can start getting an idea of how bad they are and start addressing them as we go. Start creating guardrails to protect society and the planet. And once we have this information, companies can use it in order to say, OK, we're going to choose this model because it's more sustainable, this model because it respects copyright. Legislators who really need information to write laws, can use these tools to develop new regulation mechanisms or governance for AI as it gets deployed into society. And users like you and me can use this information to choose AI models that we can trust, not to misrepresent us and not to misuse our data. But what did I reply to that email that said that my work is going to destroy humanity? I said that focusing on AI's future existential risks is a distraction from its current, very tangible impacts and the work we should be doing right now, or even yesterday, for reducing these impacts. Because yes, AI is moving quickly, but it's not a done deal. We're building the road as we walk it, and we can collectively decide what direction we want to go in together. Thank you. (Applause)

transcript: In January 2024, just days before the New Hampshire primary, thousands of registered Democrats answered their phones to hear a familiar voice. It sounded exactly like President Joe Biden, down to his specific cadence. The voice told them to save their vote for November and skip the primary. But the audio was a digital clone. Joe Biden never recorded that message. A political consultant later admitted to commissioning the call using AI voice technology to target voters in New Hampshire and was one of the first confirmed uses of a digital clone to actively suppress an American electorate. The New Hampshire incident turned AI-generated voice technology into a functional tool for voter suppression. Deception through digital synthesis had moved from a prediction into an active campaign tactic. This single event proved that a synthetic recording could successfully intervene in a presidential primary, challenging the basic assumption that hearing a candidate's voice is a guarantee of their presence. This capability is driven by generative adversarial networks, or GANs. Inside these models, two programs compete. One generates a forgery and the other attempts to detect it. They repeat this cycle millions of times until the AI creates an output that can bypass human detection. Historically, this level of manipulation was the domain of high-budget film crews and specialized editing suites. Producing a deepfake now requires only a consumer-grade graphics card and a few minutes of processing. The technical barrier to entry has dropped to the point where these tools are accessible to anyone with an internet connection. The collapse of financial and technical barriers made digital forgeries a constant presence in global politics. In June 2023, the Ron DeSantis campaign released an attack ad targeting Donald Trump. The ad featured AI-generated images of the former president in fabricated scenarios embracing controversial figures. By including generated images of Dr. Anthony Fauci, the campaign used AI to visually link the two figures in a way that never happened. From global parliamentary contests to targeting minority voting blocks, the digital ghost of New Hampshire became a global template for influence. If AI is sophisticated enough to build these fakes, a logical question follows. Why isn't AI sophisticated enough to catch them? Tech giants like Meta have attempted to solve this through the Deep Fake Detection Challenge using over 100,000 clips to train detection algorithms. Despite the scale of the project, researchers admit that reliable detection remains an unsolved problem. Detection software typically looks for biological anomalies such as unnatural skin textures or eye movements. However, standard social media video compression often destroys these subtle clues, allowing the forgery to be blurred into the pixels. Digital forensics expert Dr. Hany Farid warns we are decades away from having technology that can conclusively tell a real video from a fake one. Right now, no technical solution exists to protect the public. The defense is consistently outpaced by generative models, leaving the audience without a reliable filter. Deep fakes introduce a dangerous secondary threat to our elections, the ability to easily dismiss authentic evidence as a digital forgery. This is known as the liar's dividend. Technical labeling systems like C2PA aim to cryptographically verify media, but these can be bypassed by bad actors who simply strip the metadata away before sharing the file. With algorithms failing and regulations stalled, the final line of defense is individual media literacy. These digital attacks rely on bypassing logic to trigger an emotional reaction. An Atlanta Fed paper found 90% of executives admit AI has not boosted productivity at their companies yet. So, what does this mean for how you evaluate tech right now? First, assume every political message you scroll past contains unlabeled synthetic content. Second, if your team is deploying generative tools to {slash} headcount, factor in the maintenance tax before cutting staff. And third, when massive new benchmarks drop, look at who supplied the testing data before accepting the headline claims. The flood of synthetic campaign ads shows how fast deployment outruns governance, even while top tech companies struggle with the hidden cleanup costs. The question is no longer whether AI can make convincing content. It is whether our institutions can handle what happens after we press publish.
